scenes.narration: Picture the biggest IOU on Earth. It's signed by the United States government. It's so long that nobody has ever read the whole thing. And every single day, on average, about six point eight billion dollars more gets added at the bottom.

On November thirteenth, the Treasury's own daily count, called Debt to the Penny, stood at forty point six trillion dollars. So who actually holds this IOU? Most people would guess China. Most people would be wrong. China holds about a penny and a half of every dollar. So who holds the rest?
Let's open the vault. We'll meet the buyers, the dinner guests, the warehouse that bought trillions, and the filing cabinet full of Social Security's IOUs. Then we'll check the meter.

First, what is this debt? It's every Treasury security the government has issued and not yet paid back. It comes in two pieces. Thirty-two point eight trillion dollars is debt held by the public. Bills, notes and bonds that investors bought. The other seven point eight trillion dollars is debt the government owes to itself, to its own trust funds.

keyframes.cue: is debt held by the public
keyframes.label: items[2].slices[0].at.cue

scenes.narration: Let me draw it. Here's the whole IOU. Now split it. The big box is held by the public. That means anyone outside the federal government, and that includes the Federal Reserve. The smaller box is intragovernmental. Social Security's trust funds hold about a third of it, by our calculation. Hold on to that box. We'll open it later.

And it keeps growing. One year earlier, the total was thirty-eight point two trillion dollars. That's about two and a half trillion dollars added in twelve months, or roughly six point eight billion dollars a day, by our calculation. The counter passed thirty-eight trillion in October twenty twenty-five, thirty-nine trillion in March, and forty trillion on August eighteenth.

So where does new debt come from? An auction. In fiscal year twenty twenty-six, the Treasury held four hundred and thirty-six auctions, and sold nearly thirty-three trillion dollars of securities, by our count. Most of that was short-term bills, paid off and sold again, over and over.

Take one sale. On August twelfth, the Treasury auctioned forty-two billion dollars of ten-year notes, and bids came in for more than twice that. Of what the bidders won, about three quarters went to indirect bidders, who bid through a dealer. That group includes foreign central banks. Direct bidders took about fifteen percent. Big dealer banks took the rest.

And a lot of that paper is short-dated. At the end of October, Treasury bills, which mature within a year, made up almost a quarter of the marketable debt held by the public, by our calculation. Short paper has to be refinanced quickly. Remember that when we get to the interest bill.
The buyers line up every week. But who ends up holding the paper?

Picture every foreign holder at one long dinner table. In August twenty twenty-six, according to the Treasury's international capital data, foreigners held nine point three trillion dollars of Treasury securities. The biggest plate at the table isn't China's. It's Japan's, at one point zero seven trillion dollars. Second, the United Kingdom, at one point zero one trillion dollars.

China comes third, with five hundred and ninety-one billion dollars. And its plate has been shrinking. Back in twenty thirteen, China held one point three trillion dollars. Today, it holds less than half of that.

Now compare that with the whole IOU. China's holdings are about one and a half percent of the total debt, by our calculation. About a penny and a half of every dollar. All foreign holders together, about twenty-three percent. The idea that China owns America simply isn't what the data show.

Let me chart it. China in twenty thirteen, a tall bar. China today, less than half as tall. Japan today, the largest foreign holder. Now, for scale, the whole debt. All three bars fit in one corner of it.

One caveat. The Treasury itself warns that these numbers follow where securities are held in custody, not always who really owns them. Bonds kept in places like Belgium, Luxembourg or the Cayman Islands may belong to investors from somewhere else. So the guest list is a good map, not a perfect one.

About three point eight trillion dollars of the foreign total sits with official holders, mostly central banks, which keep Treasuries as reserves. When a country needs safe dollars in a hurry, this is the pantry it opens.

So if roughly three quarters of the debt isn't foreign, who holds it? Mostly, Americans. Here's the Federal Reserve's own breakdown, at the end of June twenty twenty-six, for Treasuries held outside the federal government.

Money market funds held three point three trillion dollars. That's where many people park their cash. Households held two point eight trillion dollars directly. Mutual funds and exchange-traded funds, about two point six trillion dollars.

Banks and credit unions held about two trillion dollars. State and local governments, one point six trillion dollars. Pension funds, one point two trillion dollars. And insurance companies, about six hundred billion dollars.

So if you have a retirement plan, a pension, a money market fund or a bank account, there's a decent chance a slice of this IOU is working for you. The interest the government pays doesn't vanish. A lot of it lands in American accounts.

Let me draw the loop. You put savings into a fund. The fund lends to the Treasury by buying a bond. The Treasury pays interest back to the fund. And the fund pays you. One person's debt is another person's savings.

Then there's the biggest single holder in the country. The Federal Reserve. On November eleventh, the Fed held four point six trillion dollars in Treasury securities, stacked in the warehouse of its balance sheet.

That's down from a peak of five point eight trillion dollars in June twenty twenty-two. After the pandemic, the Fed let bonds mature without replacing them all, and the shelves thinned out. But over the past year, its holdings of short-term bills grew by about three hundred and eighty-two billion dollars.
Add it up, roughly. Foreign holders, about a quarter. The Fed, about a ninth. Other investors, mostly American, close to half. And the last big piece? The one the government owes to itself.

Meet the filing cabinet. For years, Social Security collected more than it paid out in benefits. The surplus was lent to the Treasury, in exchange for special Treasury securities held only inside the government. IOUs, filed in a drawer.

At the end of twenty twenty-five, those trust fund reserves held two point five six trillion dollars, according to the trustees, as reported by the Congressional Research Service. But in twenty twenty-five, costs beat revenue, and the reserves shrank by one hundred and sixty billion dollars.

Let me draw the round trip. Payroll taxes flow into the trust fund. Any surplus goes to the Treasury, which hands back an IOU. When benefits cost more than taxes bring in, the fund hands the IOU back, and the Treasury pays cash. To find that cash, it borrows from the public.

keyframes.cue: the fund hands the IOU back
keyframes.label: strokes[6].start.cue

scenes.narration: Notice what happens to the total. Nothing, at first. The IOU just moves from the small box to the big box. Debt the government owed itself becomes debt it owes investors.

And the drawer won't last forever. The trustees project the retirement fund's reserves run out in late twenty thirty-two. Counting the disability fund too, the combined reserves last into twenty thirty-four. After that, incoming taxes would cover about eighty-three percent of scheduled benefits, unless Congress changes the law.

Which brings us to the meter. In fiscal year twenty twenty-six, which ended in September, the government's net interest bill, what it pays in interest minus what it collects, reached one point zero five trillion dollars, according to the Monthly Treasury Statement. That's about two point nine billion dollars every day, by our calculation.

Now put national defense on the other side of the scale. Same year, same statement. Nine hundred and sixty-five billion dollars. Interest outweighed it. And it wasn't a one-off. In fiscal twenty twenty-five, interest was nine hundred and seventy billion dollars, and defense, nine hundred and seventeen billion dollars.

Why did the meter speed up? Rates. In October twenty twenty-one, the average interest rate on the government's marketable debt was one point four six percent. By October twenty twenty-six, it was three point five seven percent. Cheap old bonds keep maturing, and they get replaced with pricier new ones.

Let me put them side by side. Defense, fiscal twenty twenty-six. Net interest, a bit taller. Medicare, about the same height as interest. Social Security, taller still. Interest is now about fourteen cents of every federal dollar spent, by our calculation.

And remember who sits on the other end of that meter. The holders we met tonight. Money funds, pensions, banks, households, the Fed, and investors abroad. Every tick of the meter is a payment to somebody.

And the Congressional Budget Office expects the meter to keep speeding up. In its February baseline, net interest climbs from three point three percent of the economy this year to four point six percent by twenty thirty-six. The previous high, going back to nineteen forty, was three point two percent, in nineteen ninety-one. That's a projection, not a result.

So who actually owns America's debt? Not China, at least not much of it. Foreign investors hold about a quarter, and Japan holds more than China. The Fed holds about a ninth. The government owes almost a fifth to itself, mostly to future retirees. And most of the rest belongs to Americans, through money funds, banks, pensions and their own savings. The biggest lender to the United States is the United States. So every dollar of interest is two things at once. A cost for taxpayers, and income for whoever holds the IOU.
